headline: Big 5 Construct Saudi 2026: What to Expect in Riyadh
deck: The conference agenda is organised around the things that go wrong on Saudi projects: code compliance, concrete quality, governance and the handover between trades.
excerpt: The conference programme for Big 5 Construct Saudi covers codes and standards, health and safety, sustainability, artificial intelligence, technology, project management, concrete, modular construction and HVACR. Speaking organisations include the Saudi Building Code Center, ROSHN Group, Saudi Binladin Group, Misk City and Kabbani Construction Group.
content:
Big 5 Construct Saudi opens at the Riyadh Front Exhibition & Conference Center on 30 August, and the programme running alongside the exhibition floor is a reasonable guide to what the Saudi industry currently considers its own weak points.

The topic areas are codes, standards and regulations; health and safety; sustainability; artificial intelligence; technology; project management; concrete; modular construction; and HVACR. Individual sessions address navigating the Saudi Building Code, improving concrete quality, strengthening project governance, applying artificial intelligence in project delivery, and improving coordination between HVACR design, installation and facilities management.

That is not a list of emerging technologies. It is a list of delivery failures. Concrete quality, code navigation, governance and the design-to-operation handover are the four places where Saudi projects most reliably lose time and money, and the programme has been built around them rather than around product categories.

The organisations speaking reflect the same emphasis. They include the Saudi Building Code Center, ROSHN Group, SEVEN, Misk City, Saudi Binladin Group, Kabbani Construction Group, Al Kholi Group, Modern Building Leaders and Dussman Ajlan & Bros. That mix puts the regulator, the giga-project clients, the large domestic contractors and the facilities management operators in the same programme, which is unusual: these groups normally meet in a procurement negotiation rather than on a panel.

Among the named speakers are Christopher Seymour, managing director for the Middle East and Africa at Mace Consult, and Shonagh Kinnaird MCIOB, project director at Misk City. Their sessions examine collaboration between stakeholders, digital transparency, procurement challenges and lessons drawn from Saudi Arabia's major developments.

Digital transparency is the phrase worth pausing on. Saudi packages have become fewer and much larger, with the average award roughly doubling in size over the past year and delivery horizons stretching toward 2029 and 2030. On a five-year programme with dozens of interfaces, the question of who can see what data, when, stops being an IT matter and becomes the mechanism by which a claim is either avoided or won.

The exhibition itself is organised around the heavy end of a project, with four co-located shows: Heavy Saudi Arabia for equipment, Totally Concrete Saudi Arabia, HVACR Saudi Arabia, and Saudi FM & Clean for facilities management and cleaning. The organiser expects more than 1,000 exhibitors from over 50 countries and more than 35,000 trade visitors across the four days, running to 2 September. The visitor figure is a target rather than an outcome.

The sector mix is what distinguishes the event from a property exhibition. Heavy equipment, concrete, cooling and maintenance are the categories a contractor buys rather than the ones a developer markets, and the buyers who matter on that floor are procurement managers, plant managers and technical directors rather than sales agents.

The event runs under the patronage of the Ministry of Industry and Mineral Resources, which places it inside the Kingdom's industrial policy rather than its housing or municipal policy. Given how much of the construction supply chain has been localised in the past five years, and how much of the remaining opportunity is in localising more of it, that is a more accurate home for the exhibition than it would have been a decade ago.

For visitors, the practical planning point is that the conference sessions and the exhibition halls compete for the same four days. The programme is heavily weighted toward the first two, and the concrete, HVACR and facilities management tracks run in parallel rather than in sequence, so a technical team covering more than one discipline will need to split.
